Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 24; all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; MDMA taken on at least 5 earlier occasions). Two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, with MDMA 100 mg on day 3, 3 hours after that day's capsule. A 13th man was withdrawn after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety) and never took MDMA.

Ratings of bad effects, fear, and depression or sadness did not change significantly with paroxetine (nor with MDMA alone), and no hallucinations, psychotic symptoms or serious adverse events were seen. The authors write that the marked decrease in positive effects may lead to higher MDMA doses (they give people with depression who take SSRIs as an example) and so to potentially life-threatening toxicity; no extra MDMA was given in the study, so this is their inference. The abstract gives the rise in MDMA level as 30%, a figure taken in the Discussion from an earlier 7-man analysis; the trial's own figures are 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure to 21 hours).

Outcome: a recorded potentially unsafe driver action (proxy for responsibility), so the comparison is among drivers already in fatal crashes. THC is a yes/no blood marker of unstated analyte with no concentration, dose or timing; the authors note THC can remain in the blood for hours or days and that FARS does not say why THC was present. evidence_set: The Hunter Area Toxicology Service is a regional toxicology unit; every overdose presentation and admission is entered prospectively into a clinical database by two trained staff who were blind to the hypotheses. Of 9960 admissions between 13 January 1987 and 22 November 2002, 2222 involved at least one serotonergic drug taken in overdose; this test dataset had no exclusions and includes the derivation dataset. Derivation dataset: 473 admissions with a single SSRI, after excluding 9 with two SSRIs and any with a tricyclic antidepressant, MAOI, venlafaxine, nefazodone, lithium or an anti-serotonergic drug taken as well. Of the 473, 73 (15.4%, 95%CI 12.3–19.0) had a diagnosis of serotonin toxicity made by a clinical toxicologist, 70 (14.8%, 95%CI 11.7–18.4) met Sternbach's criteria and 44 (9.3%, 95%CI 6.8–12.3) were treated with a 5-HT2A antagonist. The tree analysis was done in the SSRI-alone dataset; the rules were tested on the complete dataset. The paper reports no age values, sex, breakdown by drug or amounts (age was tested, p = 0.004, with no direction given).

The review calls generalised clonus (inducible, spontaneous, ocular) the classic feature and the key component of the Hunter criteria, which it says have been validated and can be used to confirm moderate or severe toxicity; the only source cited for this statement is the derivation paper (reference 13). It describes spontaneous clonus as rhythmic, large muscle contractions, often triggered by minor movements or vibrations; it says clonus in general is easily elicited with ankle dorsiflexion; and it describes ocular clonus as fine or coarse oscillations of gaze in all directions.
